strengths: Clearly identifies and empirically demonstrates two concrete failure modes of prior context-adaptation methods (brevity bias and context collapse), including a compelling case study (Figure 2) showing a sharp accuracy/token collapse in Dynamic Cheatsheet.

Broad and fairly rigorous empirical evaluation spanning offline (system prompt) and online (test-time memory) adaptation across agent (AppWorld) and domain-specific (FiNER, Formula) benchmarks, with consistent, sizable gains (10.6% agents, 8.6% finance) over multiple strong baselines (ICL, MIPROv2, GEPA, Dynamic Cheatsheet).

Practical significance is well supported: substantial reductions in rollouts, latency (up to ~91.5%), and dollar cost compared to GEPA/DC, plus a leaderboard comparison showing a smaller open-source model matching/surpassing a GPT-4.1-based production agent.
Good ablation study isolating the contribution of the Reflector, multi-epoch refinement, and offline warmup, supporting the claimed design choices.

High transparency/reproducibility effort: full prompts for Generator/Reflector/Curator and baselines are released in the appendix, and the method is described in enough detail (bullet metadata, delta updates, grow-and-refine) to reimplement.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: ACE is explicitly built on top of Dynamic Cheatsheet's agentic architecture, and the core new ideas (itemized bullets, delta updates, dedup via embeddings, separate reflector) are largely engineering refinements of existing memory/context frameworks (A-MEM, DC, GEPA) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Evaluation is limited to a single base LLM family (DeepSeek-V3.1) and a narrow domain-specific application (financial XBRL tasks); generality of the 'domain-specific benchmark' claims and robustness across different model scales/architectures is untested.

Results without ground-truth labels are inconsistent: in Table 2, ACE without GT/execution signals sometimes underperforms the base LLM (e.g., FiNER online -3.4), undercutting the abstract's claim that ACE 'could adapt effectively without labeled supervision,' which appears true mainly for agent tasks with rich execution feedback but not more generally.

No variance/multiple-seed reporting; all numbers appear to be single-run results, raising concerns about the statistical reliability of the reported gains, especially given the relatively small absolute differences in some ablations.

Comparison to baselines could be seen as somewhat asymmetric since ACE contexts are substantially longer (thousands of tokens) than the concise prompts produced by GEPA/MIPROv2 by design; while the paper argues long-context serving costs are amortized, no direct inference-time latency/cost comparison for using the resulting (longer) ACE context at serving time is provided, only adaptation-time costs.

The AppWorld leaderboard comparison is a moving-target, timestamped snapshot (Sept 2025) that may not be reproducible/verifiable by future readers, weakening the strength of this particular claim over time.

strengths: Addresses a clearly motivated and well-illustrated problem (brevity bias and context collapse), with a concrete empirical demonstration (Figure 2) that grounds the paper's core claims.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning multiple task types (agentic AppWorld, financial reasoning, medical reasoning, text-to-SQL) and multiple LLM backbones (DeepSeek-V3.1, GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-5.1, Llama-3.3-70B), showing the method generalizes across models and domains.
Strong and consistent performance gains over reasonably strong baselines (ICL, MIPROv2, GEPA, Dynamic Cheatsheet) in both offline and online adaptation settings.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of the Reflector, multi-epoch adaptation, incremental delta updates, and hyperparameter sensitivity (dedup threshold, pruning trigger, reflection iterations).
Practical, systems-level cost/latency analysis (rollouts, tokens, KV-cache reuse) that meaningfully addresses concerns about the practicality of long, evolving contexts.
Additional analyses on robustness to noisy/harmful reflection and weaker Reflector models strengthen the credibility of the approach's robustness claims.
Detailed prompts and experimental settings are provided in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is somewhat incremental: ACE is explicitly built on top of Dynamic Cheatsheet's agentic architecture, and the main additions (separate Reflector role, delta updates, grow-and-refine merging) are largely engineering refinements rather than fundamentally new algorithmic ideas; overlap with existing agent-memory frameworks (A-MEM, AWM) is only briefly discussed.

Reported results appear to be from single runs without variance/multiple-seed reporting, which is concerning given the benchmarks (especially AppWorld) are known to be noisy; this makes it hard to assess the statistical significance of the reported gains.

The comparison against IBM CUGA on the AppWorld leaderboard is prominently featured in the abstract/intro as a headline result, but the paper itself caveats that it is not a controlled, apples-to-apples comparison (different agent architectures, tools, and models), creating some tension between the marketing framing and the acknowledged limitations.

The central thesis that 'more comprehensive, longer contexts are better' is contradicted by the paper's own discussion (e.g., HotpotQA, Game of 24 needing concise contexts), suggesting the generality of the claimed insight is narrower than implied by the abstract.

Fairness of baseline comparisons is only partially addressed: ACE consumes substantially more input tokens at evaluation time than GEPA baselines, and while KV-cache reuse arguments are offered to mitigate this, actual cost may vary substantially depending on deployment/serving infrastructure and is not universally guaranteed.

The offline ACE variant with ground-truth labels is compared to GEPA/MIPROv2 also using labels, but the framing sometimes conflates label-free and label-based results, which could confuse readers about when ACE truly operates without supervision.

No systematic study of how the accumulated playbook scales or degrades over very long adaptation horizons (beyond the 80-step case study), nor a human evaluation of the claimed interpretability of the resulting bulleted playbooks.
